strengths: Conceptual framing: The paper presents an intuitive and elegant bridge connecting feature-space out-of-distribution (OOD) detection techniques (specifically NCI and fDBD) to hallucination detection in LLMs by viewing next-token prediction through a classification geometry lens.

Practical problem setting: The proposed framework is single-sample and training-free, circumventing both the distribution-shift vulnerabilities of probe/classifier-based approaches and the high inference overhead of multi-sample consistency approaches.

Pragmatic adaptations for LLM scale: The paper explicitly tackles two major computational and statistical roadblocks in applying OOD methods to LLMs: estimating the training feature mean without access to pre-training corpora (Decision-Neutral Closest Point) and scaling distance calculations across massive vocabularies via top-k candidate restriction.

Solid empirical performance: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks (CSQA, GSM8K, AQuA) and model families/scales (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-3-32B) show consistent improvements in AUROC over strong single-sample and multi-sample baselines, alongside useful sensitivity and temperature ablation studies.
weaknesses: Trivialization of the analytical proxy under modern architectures: The paper develops a formal derivation for the decision-neutral closest point $z^*$ (Lemma 4.1), but modern autoregressive LLMs (such as Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5) operate with zero bias ($b = 0$) in their unembedding heads. As noted by the authors, $z^*$ trivially reduces to the origin $\mathbf{0}$. While setting $\mu_G = 0$ works empirically, the theoretical derivation for $z^*$ provides little practical value for the tested models beyond simply zero-centering.

Narrow benchmark scope: The empirical evaluation is restricted to reasoning and multiple-choice benchmarks (CSQA, GSM8K, AQuA). Given that hallucination is an established problem in open-ended generation, factual knowledge retrieval (e.g., TriviaQA, PopQA, TruthfulQA), and document summarization/grounded QA (e.g., HaluEval), it remains unclear whether these geometric metrics generalize beyond step-by-step reasoning chains.

Heuristic sequence-level aggregation: The token-level geometric uncertainty scores are simply averaged uniformly across the entire generated sequence ($S = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t} s(z^t)$). In multi-step reasoning, uninformative filler words, syntax tokens, and punctuation may dilute the signal from crucial logical or numerical pivot tokens.

Lack of wall-clock latency measurements: Although theoretical asymptotic complexity is analyzed ($O(d_{\text{model}} k + |V|)$ per step), evaluating the metric at every generation step incurs additional memory and compute overhead over standard logits. Reporting actual wall-clock inference latency comparisons against standard single-sample baselines (such as Perplexity and MaxP) would substantiate the efficiency claims.

strengths: Conceptual Perspective: Connecting token-level uncertainty and hallucination detection to geometric out-of-distribution (OOD) metrics (specifically feature-to-weight proximity and distance-to-decision-boundary) provides an intuitive geometric viewpoint on LLM generation.

Efficiency and Scalability: The proposed adaptations are single-sample and training-free, avoiding the heavy computational cost of multi-sample consistency approaches and the overhead of training separate verifiers/probes.

Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation: The authors evaluate on three datasets (CSQA, GSM8K, AQuA) across different model families and scales (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Qwen-3-32B), demonstrating consistent AUROC gains over standard predictive confidence and multi-sample baselines.
Practical Ablations: The paper provides informative ablations regarding the choice of candidate set size $k$ and verifies robustness under various stochastic sampling temperatures.
weaknesses: Conflation of Hallucination with Reasoning Correctness: The paper evaluates exclusively on reasoning benchmarks (CSQA, GSM8K, AQuA) and treats any incorrect response as a 'hallucination'. In multi-step mathematical and logical reasoning, errors frequently arise from arithmetic mistakes or flawed deduction rather than out-of-distribution semantic hallucinations. The absence of standard hallucination benchmarks (e.g., HaluEval, TruthfulQA, FactScore, or open-domain factual generation) makes the central claim overly broad.

Limited Methodological Novelty: The core formulations (NCI and fDBD) are imported directly from prior work (Liu & Qin, 2024; 2025). The primary adaptation to LLMs consists of: (1) an analytical feature mean proxy which simply reduces to the origin ($0$) for modern zero-bias language heads, (2) restricting boundary distances to the top-$k$ logits (a standard heuristic), and (3) simple uniform sequence-level averaging.

Flawed Tightness Claim for Theorem 3.3: In Appendix C, the authors state that the lower bound in Eq. (3) is 'tight'. While the Euclidean distance from a point to a separating hyperplane between two classes has a closed form, the Euclidean distance to a multi-class Voronoi decision region $R_c$ is equal to this hyperplane distance if and only if the projection of $z$ onto the hyperplane lies within the closure of $R_c$. In high-dimensional spaces with $|V| > 10^5$, this condition rarely holds for arbitrary candidates $c$. Claiming general tightness across alternative tokens is mathematically incorrect.

Trivialization of the Analytical Proxy: The derivation of the 'Decision-Neutral Closest Point' in Lemma 4.1 / Appendix D is framed as a key technical resolution to the lack of training statistics. However, as noted in Section 4.2, modern LLMs (e.g., Llama and Qwen families) do not use bias terms ($b = 0$). Consequently, the analytical proxy $\hat{z}^*$ identically evaluates to $0$. The empirical improvement of the 'analytical proxy' over empirical centering in Table 1 simply reflects that uncentered features ($z - 0$) outperform subtracting an ad-hoc task mean.

Naive Sequence Aggregation: Simply taking the arithmetic mean of step-wise scores across the entire generated sequence ignores the varying informational importance of different tokens (e.g., function words and template tokens vs. critical reasoning steps).
Incomplete Citations: Several in-text citations are missing publication years or complete metadata, such as '(Azaria & Mitchell; ... Liu et al.; ... Marks & Tegmark; ...)' in Sections 1 and 6.

strengths: Conceptual framing: Connecting out-of-distribution (OOD) geometric uncertainty metrics (feature proximity and decision boundary distance) to hallucination detection in LLMs offers an intuitive and interesting perspective.

Training-free and single-sample: The approach avoids training auxiliary probing models or generating multiple sample paths, making it computationally lightweight at inference time compared to consistency-based methods.

Consistent empirical gains over perplexity: Across multiple datasets (CSQA, GSM8K, AQuA) and model scales (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-3-32B), the adapted metrics (NCI and fDBD) show clear AUROC improvements over standard perplexity and predictive probability baselines.

Pragmatic top-k adaptation: Restricting boundary distance computations to top-k candidate tokens addresses the computational bottleneck caused by LLMs' large vocabulary sizes, and the sensitivity analysis demonstrates that performance is robust across variations of k.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The underlying uncertainty metrics, NCI and fDBD, are directly ported from prior OOD literature (Liu & Qin, 2024; 2025). The sequence-level extension is an unweighted arithmetic mean across decoding steps, leaving the core technical contribution relatively incremental.

Trivial reduction of the theoretical proxy: A substantial portion of Section 4.2 and Appendix D is dedicated to deriving the analytical proxy for the feature mean via the 'Decision-Neutral Closest Point' (Lemma 4.1). However, as the authors acknowledge, modern LLMs (including all models evaluated: LLaMA and Qwen) use zero-bias linear heads (b = 0), which renders this entire derivation equivalent to simply setting the feature center to the origin (0). Dedicating substantial space to a derivation that has no operational effect in the empirical evaluation is misleading.

Missing crucial margin baselines and ablations: In Eq. (3) and Eq. (6), the fDBD metric is essentially a logit difference normalized by feature norm and weight vector distance, i.e., (logit_c_hat - logit_c) / (||w_c_hat - w_c||_2 * ||z^t||_2). The paper lacks essential ablations isolating whether the empirical improvements stem from the raw logit margin (top-1 vs top-2 logit difference), the feature norm ||z^t||_2, or the denominator weight distance. Simple confidence baselines such as sequence-average Shannon entropy, minimum token probability, and logit/softmax margin are conspicuously absent.

Underpowered multi-sample baseline settings: The multi-sample baselines (e.g., Semantic Entropy, SelfCheckGPT-NLI) are run with only 3 samples, which is widely recognized as too few for semantic clustering and divergence estimation to stabilize. Discrediting sample-consistency approaches in reasoning based on this constrained setting is not sufficiently justified.

Presentation flaws and citation errors: There are several broken citations and incomplete sentences in the text, such as 'Azaria & Mitchell;' (p. 1), 'Liu et al.;' (p. 1), 'Marks & Tegmark;' (p. 1), Perplexity listed twice under baselines (p. 6), and a truncated sentence on page 12 ('We focus on three computationally efficient As shown in Table 6').
